     THE NEAR FRATTINI SUBGROUP OF A KNOT GROUP IS
                         TRIVIAL

                                        GROUPTHEORY50


        Abstract. We prove that the near Frattini subgroup of every knot group is trivial.
        The argument first identifies the lower and upper near Frattini subgroups for finitely
        generated groups, and then shows that every nontrivial element of a finitely generated
        torsion-free virtually RFRS group is a near generator. Virtual specialness of knot
        groups then gives the result. This answers both parts of Problem 19.1 of the Kourovka
        Notebook.




                                       1. Introduction
   The Frattini subgroup packages nongenerators of a group. The near Frattini variants
replace generation by finite-index generation and are therefore adapted to infinite groups.
Problem 19.1 of the Kourovka Notebook, proposed by M. K. Azarian, asks whether the
near Frattini subgroup is trivial for groups of composite knots and for cable knot groups
[3]. We prove the stronger statement for every knot group.
   The topological input is the now-standard virtual-specialness theory for compact
3-manifolds with boundary, together with Agol’s RFRS framework [1, 2, 4, 5]. The
group-theoretic reduction is elementary and may be useful in other settings.

                               2. Near Frattini subgroups
  An element x ∈ G is a non-near generator if, for every S ⊆ G,
                           [G : hS, xi] < ∞      =⇒      [G : hSi] < ∞.
Let λ(G) be the set of non-near generators. A subgroup is nearly maximal if it is
maximal among the infinite-index subgroups, and let µ(G) be the intersection of all
nearly maximal subgroups. If λ(G) = µ(G), their common value is denoted ψ(G).
Lemma 2.1. The set λ(G) is a characteristic subgroup of G.
Proof. The identity and inverses are immediate. Suppose x, y ∈ λ(G) and hS, xyi has
finite index. Then hS, x, yi has finite index. Applying the defining property first to x
with S ∪ {y}, and then to y with S, shows that hSi has finite index. Automorphism
invariance is immediate from the definition.                                          
Theorem 2.2. If G is finitely generated, then λ(G) = µ(G).
Proof. By Lemma 2.1, λ(G) is a subgroup of G. If g ∈ λ(G) and M is nearly maximal,
then g ∈ / M would imply that hM, gi has finite index and therefore, by the non-near
property, that M has finite index. Hence λ(G) ≤ µ(G).
   Conversely, let g ∈ / λ(G). There is an infinite-index subgroup L such that hL, gi has
finite index. Consider the poset of infinite-index subgroups containing L. The union of a
chain still has infinite index: otherwise the union would be a finite-index subgroup of the
  Date: August 27, 2026.

finitely generated group G, hence finitely generated, and its generators would already lie
in a single member of the chain. Zorn’s lemma gives a nearly maximal subgroup M ≥ L.
Since hL, gi has finite index, one has g ∈
                                         / M . Thus g ∈/ µ(G).                          

                                            3. RFRS groups
     For a group H write
                              Hr(1) = ker H −→ Hab ⊗Z Q .
                                                                       

A finitely generated group is RFRS if it admits a separating chain of finite-index normal
subgroups
                        H = H0 ≥ H1 ≥ · · · ,     (Hi )r(1) ≤ Hi+1 .
Theorem 3.1. If G is finitely generated, torsion-free, and virtually RFRS, then ψ(G) =
1.
Proof. By Theorem 2.2, ψ(G) is defined. Let 1 6= g ∈ G, and choose a finite-index RFRS
subgroup H ≤ G. Some positive power x = g m lies in H, and torsion-freeness gives
x 6= 1.
   Take an RFRS chain (Hi ). Since it is separating, choose i with x ∈ Hi \ Hi+1 . As
     (1)
(Hi )r ≤ Hi+1 , the image of x in Hiab ⊗ Q is nonzero. Hence there is a homomorphism
χ : Hi → Z with χ(x) 6= 0. Put L = ker χ. Then L has infinite index in Hi , whereas
Lhxi has finite index in Hi . Since Hi has finite index in G and x is a power of g, the
subgroup hL, gi has finite index in G. Thus g ∈/ λ(G). No nontrivial element belongs to
λ(G), so ψ(G) = 1.                                                                   

                                            4. Knot groups
Theorem 4.1. Let K ⊂ S 3 be a knot and let GK = π1 (S 3 \ νK). Then
                                                ψ(GK ) = 1.
Proof. Knot groups are finitely generated and torsion-free. The unknot group is infinite
cyclic, for which the conclusion is immediate. For every nontrivial knot, the virtual-
specialness results for hyperbolic, graph-manifold-with-boundary, and mixed 3-manifold
pieces imply that GK is virtually special [2, 4, 5]; virtually special groups are virtually
RFRS [1]. Theorem 3.1 applies.                                                           
Corollary 4.2. As a consequence of Theorem 4.1, the answer to both parts of Kourovka
Problem 19.1 is affirmative. In fact the conclusion holds for all knot groups, not only
groups of composite or cable knots.

                                             5. Perspective
  The proof separates the problem into a purely algebraic statement and a geometric
source of RFRS chains. Consequently Theorem 3.1 applies well beyond knot groups:
every finitely generated torsion-free virtually RFRS group has trivial near Frattini
subgroup.
